1	# Running tests
2	
3	**track**
4	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testFast`.
5	
6	**shard**
7	: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.
8	
9	**code state**
10	: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.
11	
12	## The two suites
13	
14	`ant testFast` runs about 1,800 tests in four tracks at once, in about 9 to 11 minutes:
15	
16	- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
17	- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
18	- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
19	- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes.
20	
21	`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs about 500 tests in four shards, in about 2 to 4 minutes.
22	
23	`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in under a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.
24	
25	The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:
26	
27	    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'
28	
29	The two suites work in the same way:
30	
31	- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
32	- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
33	- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
34	- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.
35	
36	To run a suite:
37	
38	- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
39	- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
40	- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
41	- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.
42	
43	## The switches that the harness reads
44	
45	Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.
46	
47	- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
48	- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
49	- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
50	- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
51	- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
52	- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.
53	
54	## Outside the gate
55	
56	- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
57	- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).
58	
59	## When to run a whole suite
60	
61	- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
62	- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
63	  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
64	  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
65	  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`) or the parser, run both.
66	- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
67	- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
68	- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the run time (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
69	- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests.
70	
71	The suites do not check these:
72	
73	- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
74	- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
75	- the linker's aliasing of apis;
76	- `fortress unparse`;
77	- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
78	- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.
79	
80	If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.
81	
82	## One test, or a few
83	
84	Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.
85	
86	### Interpreter tests
87	
88	Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:
89	
90	    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
91	        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]
92	
93	- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
94	- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
95	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
96	- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
97	- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
98	- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
99	- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.
100	
101	To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:
102	
103	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss
104	
105	The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").
106	
107	### Compiled tests
108	
109	Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`).
110	
111	The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.
112	
113	    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
114	        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1
115	
116	- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
117	- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
118	- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
119	- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
120	- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
121	- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.
122	
123	To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:
124	
125	    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test
126	
127	Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.
128	
129	## One unit-test class, or one track
130	
131	To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.
132	
133	To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:
134	
135	- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
136	- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
137	- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
138	- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.

1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
42	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
43	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
44	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:
45	
46	         git push origin main
47	         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
48	         git push origin main:blinded-fable
49	
50	     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
51	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
52	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

1	# The report and the record
2	
3	## What every report holds
4	
5	Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.
6	
7	A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.
8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	Three limits of `ledger.py` (below):
55	
56	- A row at its 1,200-character limit takes no further note.
57	- No command edits a row's claim. `close --claim` takes a corrected one.
58	- Its heading reader does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
59	
60	## Reading the record
61	
62	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
63	
64	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
65	
66	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
67	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
68	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
69	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
70	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
71	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
72	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
73	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
74	
75	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
76	
77	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
78	
79	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
80	
81	## Writing to the record
82	
83	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
84	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
85	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
86	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
87	  - what it means for the work;
88	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
89	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
90	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
91	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
92	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
93	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
94	
95	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
96	
97	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
98	
99	To add a row:
100	
101	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
102	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
103	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
104	
105	To change a row:
106	
107	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N.
108	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
109	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
117	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
118	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

The rung's skeptic checks the time and the results. This work is part of the rung, not a separate step after the landing. == Specification/basic/components/type-inference.tex:12-53

\section{Type Inference for Components}
\seclabel{type-inference-components}

Type inference for Fortress has been described as a procedure performed
over a whole Fortress program in \chapref{type-inference}. In this
section, we explain how this procedure can 
be adapted to perform type inference over a simple program component. 
For a compound component,
concatenate all declarations of all constituents in
the order specified by the constructing \shellcommand{link}
operation.  Constituent compound component declarations are
recursively concatenated.


Type inference over a simple component $C$ is performed by first
expanding $C$ into a self-contained Fortress program, as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item All program constructs corresponding to declarations in APIs exported by
$C$ are expanded so that they include all types and static parameters
included in the exported APIs. 
\item All types provided by all declarations in the APIs imported by $C$
are prepended to $C$. Note that these declarations must include
types for all variables, functions, fields, and methods;
otherwise the APIs that declare them are not well-formed.
\item In order for the resulting expanded program to be well-formed, 
we assume that all declarations in these APIs are
expanded into special definitions that include \emph{empty bodies}.
The empty body of such a definition is a conceptual body which
cannot be expressed directly in Fortress programs.
Because declarations in APIs do not have any elided type,
type inference ignores empty bodies.
\end{enumerate}
Once $C$ is expanded, type inference 
is performed over all program constructs that still include elided types.
Empty bodies are ignored.
\revision{revival-paramtype}{The compiled type checker does not yet infer the
type of a parameter that a function declaration leaves out, at top level, in a
trait or object, or local to an expression block: it refuses the component
with the message ``Missing parameter type for'' followed by the parameter's
name.
The inference this paragraph asks for is not yet described
(\chapref{type-inference}).}

34	**The change.**
35	- An api's declaration for a function that leaves out its return type. The team's compiler gave such a function in a component the return type of the first api declaration of its name, whatever its parameter types (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/ApiTypeExtractor.scala:117` at a874948ac; dotted and functional methods at `:91` and `:98`). The tree takes the api declaration of the function's own parameter types, and none where several fit a declaration that leaves out a parameter type (`OmittedReturnTypeFromApi`, `OmittedMethodReturnTypeFromApi`). Reason: "Type Inference for Components" expands each construct "corresponding to declarations in APIs exported by C" with the api's types (`Specification/basic/components/type-inference.tex:29`). Measured: `opr BIG LEXICO(g)` took `BIG LEXICO()`'s `BigReduction[\TotalComparison,TotalComparison\]`, 'Function body has type TotalComparison, but declared return type is BigReduction[...]' at `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:130`, depending on the order of identity hashes.
36	- The top-level overloading check and abstract functional methods. The team's compiler checked a component's top-level overloads over declarations with a body only (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:120` at a874948ac). So an abstract functional method beside an unrelated top-level function of its name passed, where the same pair with a body was refused. The tree reads every functional method, abstract ones too, and leaves out an abstract one that a subtype's declaration implements with the same parameter types (`XXXFunctionalMethodMeetTopLevelAbstract`, `AbstractFunctionalMethodImplementedByComprised`, `AbstractFunctionalMethodOfGenericTrait`). Reason: "A valid overloading between a functional method declaration and a function declaration is determined by applying the (more restrictive) Meet Rule for functions" (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex:525-529`); walk refuses the abstract pair at load already, 'first parameters x:[String] and self:[S] are unrelated'.
37	- The per-provider message's kind word. The team's compiler called every trait or object 'trait' in 'Invalid overloading of m in trait O' (`OverloadingChecker.scala:284` at a874948ac). The tree says 'object' for an object (`XXXDottedMethodMeetAbstractSibling`). Reason: the line tested the compilation unit, which is never an object's index.
38	- The fourth row, 681, changes no team source's behaviour: the team's compiler had no size inference variables (`Formula.isNatTerm` is the revival's own, 3f297441c). The tree now does what the specification says, inferring `get[\i-1\]` (`NatArithInferChecker`).
39	
40	**Provenance.**
41	- Rows 737, 738, 739 and 681, in the order the batch 16 review gave (`explorations/reviews/batch-16-review.md`, Part 4; PLAN phase 3, item 15). Row 739 follows the reasons of P-149, and its default on the curator's list is "built in climb batch 17's checker rung". Built in climb batch 17, rung C.

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,

ledger).
\chapref{multiple-dispatch} and \chapref{overloaded-declarations} were revised
with this chapter's order, a declaration chosen on the parameter types it
declares and then instantiated (\secref{revival-overloading}).
The team's later Types chapter gives the coercion relation and the valid
instantiations of a quantified type, and says nothing of inference.}

\section{The Static Arguments of a Call}
\seclabel{static-arg-inference}

The static arguments of a call that does not write them are found in two
steps: the declaration that the call invokes is chosen first, and it is
instantiated second.

\emph{Choice.}
The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes.
A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call, without or with
coercion, if some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is
applicable to the call.
Declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare, a declaration
with static parameters on its parameter types taken over every instance that
its bounds allow, and not on an instance inferred for the call.
So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which
declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it.

\emph{Instantiation.}
The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
\begin{itemize}
\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
type of the instance.
\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
expected type as well.
\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
.....
See \chapref{trait-parameters} for a discussion of static parameters.
A static parameter may be instantiated with a type or a value
depending on whether it is a type parameter.
\note{
Victor: I don't know if the follow really belongs here.
It isn't complete in any case, because of union/intersection types.}
Two types are identical if and only if they are the same kind and
their names and static arguments (if any) are identical.
Two \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} static arguments
(\secref{natparams}, \secref{static-expr})
are identical if and only if they are written alike
once each operation whose operands are numerals is replaced by its value:
\EXP{2\;3} and \EXP{6} are identical,
and \EXP{s_{0}\;s_{1}} is identical to itself but not to \EXP{s_{1}\;s_{0}}.
Two such arguments are known to differ when they are two different numerals;
a static parameter, or an expression in which one occurs,
is not known to differ from a numeral,
since the parameter may be instantiated with a value at which they are equal.

#!/bin/bash
# run-diff.sh P [P ...]: old and new, compiled and walk, for programs in skeptic/p
W=/home/user/fortress-checkrows
SK=$W/tmp/rung-checker-four-rows/skeptic
OLD="/home/user/fortress-base17/explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base17 $W/tmp/old-caches"
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
export FORTRESS_HOME=$W FORTRESS_THREADS=${FORTRESS_THREADS:-1} TMPDIR=$W/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$W/tmp"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
cd $SK/p
for P in "$@"; do
  echo "################ $P"
  if [ -z "$NOCOMPILED" ]; then
  echo "== old compiled"; timeout 300 $OLD compile $P.fss 2>&1 | head -${LINES_MAX:-25}; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
  timeout 120 $OLD run $P 2>&1 | head -12; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
  echo "== new compiled"; FORTRESS_CACHES=$SK/new-caches timeout 300 $W/bin/fortress compile $P.fss 2>&1 | head -${LINES_MAX:-25}; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
  FORTRESS_CACHES=$SK/new-caches timeout 120 $W/bin/fortress run $P 2>&1 | head -12; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
  fi
  if [ -z "$NOWALK" ]; then
  echo "== old walk"; timeout 300 $OLD $P.fss 2>&1 | head -12; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
  echo "== new walk"; FORTRESS_CACHES=$SK/new-caches timeout 300 $W/bin/fortress $P.fss 2>&1 | head -12; echo "rc=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
  fi
done
EOF
chmod +x $SK/run-diff.sh; ls tmp/old-caches 2>/dev/null | head -2

content.content:
Export statements specify the APIs that a component exports.
One important restriction on components is that no \apiN\ may be both
imported and exported by the same component. This restriction helps to
avoid some (but not all) accidental cyclic dependencies.

Every component implicitly imports the Fortress core APIs;
every fortress has at least one component implementing all of these \apisN.
A \emph{preferred} component exporting these \apisN\ (configurable by the user)
is implicitly linked to
every component installed in the fortress.


A component must provide a declaration, or a set of declarations,
that \emph{satisfies} every top-level declaration in any API
that it exports, as described below.
A component may include declarations
that do not participate in satisfying any exported declaration
(i.e., a declaration of any exported API), and in particular,
no declaration modified by \KWD{private}
participates in satisfying any exported declaration.
Such declarations are not visible from outside the component.

Type aliases and dimension, unit, test and property declarations
are satisfied only by declarations that are the same.\footnote{The
declarations are compared after ASCII conversion and scanning,
and differences in the characters within whitespace elements
is permitted
provided they do not change whether the whitespace element
is line-breaking.
}
\note{Victor: what about trait/object/etc declarations with test modifier?}

A top-level variable declaration declaring a single variable
is satisfied by any top-level variable declaration
that declares the name with the same type
(in the component,
the type may be inferred).
A top-level variable declaration declaring multiple variables
is satisfied by a set of declarations (possibly just one)
that declare all the names with their respective types
(which again, may be inferred).
In either case,
the modifiers including the mutability of a variable must be the same in
the exported and satisfying declarations.
A top-level variable declaration
declaring a single immutable variable
with arrow type \EXP{P \rightarrow R}
is also satisfied
by a set of top-level function and functional method declarations
if the union of their parameter types is \VAR{P}
and each of their return types is a subtype of \VAR{R}.
Thus, an abstract function declaration
in the form of variable declarations in an API
need not be replicated in a component exporting that API.

A top-level function declaration is satisfied by
a set of top-level function and functional method declarations
the union of whose parameter types
is the parameter type of the exported declaration,
and each of whose return types
is a subtype of the return type of the exported declaration.
\note{Victor: also need type of thrown checked exceptions

Victor: it may also be satisfied by a declaration
 or set of declarations whose parameter type is a supertype
 of the exported declaration's parameter type
 provided that there is an overloaded exported declaration
 whose parameter type is a supertype of the satisfying declarations.
 (This comment also applied to the method declarations below.
 We need a term for this concept.)
}

1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	To weigh the specification against the team's later texts, or to find the designers' reason for a rule, read `exploring.md`, "Weighing the sources".
16	
17	## Changing the text: the revision form
18	
19	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
20	
21	1. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
22	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect. The effect names each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row.
23	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
24	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
25	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
26	
27	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
28	
29	2. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
30	
31	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
32	
33	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the entry. `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` defines `\revision`.
34	
35	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
36	
37	4. The full reasoning, in `decision-record.md` in the folder of your work under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
38	
39	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
40	
41	Check each changed sentence of `Specification/` or `Documentation/` against the curator's decisions. If it says what walk or the compiled path does, run a program that shows it.
42	
43	## Building it
44	
45	To check your LaTeX, build the specification in a built tree, after the setup lines. It takes about 90 s, so start it detached (`session.md`, "Long commands"):
46	
47	    nohup bash -c '( cd Specification/fortress && ./ant genSource && ./ant tex ) > tmp/spec.txt 2>&1; echo EXIT=$? >> tmp/spec.txt' >/dev/null 2>&1 &
48	
49	- Both commands must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and `grep -c 'Reference .* undefined\|multiply defined\|Undefined control sequence' Specification/fortress/fortress.log` must print 0.
50	- If `pdflatex` is missing, install the packages of the `PKGS` line of `explorations/experiment/setup.sh` with `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y`.
51	- The build writes only ignored files, its log among them, which can reach 400 MB. Remove them afterwards: `git clean -fXq -- Specification`.
52	- Update `Specification/fortress.pdf` only if your brief asks for it: copy `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf` over it.
53	
54	## When the text and an implementation disagree
55	
56	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, the other side is wrong. If the wrong side is in your area, change it to agree. If not, record the departure as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says.
57	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
58	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds.
59	
60	## Citing it
61	
62	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
63	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

content.content:
We say that a method declaration \emph{occurs} in a trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{declares} a method declaration that occurs
in that trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{inherits} method declarations from the
declarations of its immediate supertraits
except those method declarations
that are \emph{overridden} (as described later in this section) or
whose parameter type (not including the type of the self parameter)
is equal to the parameter type of a method declaration
that occurs in the trait declaration.
A trait declaration \emph{provides} the method declarations that it
declares or inherits.




There are two sorts of method declarations:
\emph{dotted method} declarations and
\emph{functional method} declarations.
Syntactically, a dotted method declaration is identical to a function
declaration.
When a method is invoked, a special self parameter is bound to the
object on which it is invoked.



A functional method declaration has a parameter named \KWD{self} at an
arbitrary position in its parameter list.  This parameter is not given a type
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\revision{revival-self-type}{In a trait \VAR{T} with a self-type parameter \VAR{X}
(\secref{trait-decls}), this remains the type of the \KWD{self} parameter
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks of the concrete declarations for an
abstract function declaration; one body at a narrower parameter type that does
not cover the abstract method's does not define it.
This is the rule of the type group's compiled type checker (2012) and of its
calculus Welterweight Fortress (2012).
The requirement of \secref{object-decls} that an object define all abstract
methods inherited from its supertraits is unchanged: it defines them in this
sense.}
An abstract method declaration may include the modifier \KWD{abstract}.
It may elide parameter names but parameter
types cannot be omitted except for the self parameter.


\note{
Method declarations that are overridden by some declaration are not
accessible.  They are not considered for overloading checks.

Partial overriding of an overloaded functional is allowed
but partial overriding of a functional declaration is not allowed.
}

A method declaration may have the modifier \KWD{override}.
Such a declaration \emph{overrides} any inherited declaration with the same name
and the self parameter (if any) at the same position,
whose parameter type, not counting the type of the self parameter,
is a strict subtype of the overriding declaration's parameter type.
The return type of the overriding declaration must be subtype of
that of the overridden declaration to preserve type safety.
A declaration with the modifier \KWD{override} must override
some inherited declaration.
It is a static error if a declaration with the modifier \KWD{override}
does not override any inherited declaration.

Here is an example trait \TYP{Enzyme} which provides methods
\VAR{reactionSpeed} and \VAR{catalyze}:
\input{\home/basic/examples/Trait.Method.e.tex}
\TYP{Enzyme}
inherits the abstract method \VAR{mass} from \TYP{OrganicMolecule},
declares the abstract method \VAR{reactionSpeed}, and
declares the concrete method \VAR{catalyze}
which is inherited as an abstract method
from its supertrait \TYP{Catalyst}.

They are one mechanism, row 737, which rung H found: `ApiTypeExtractor` gives `BIG LEXICO(g)` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:129-130`) the return type of the first api declaration of its name, in the identity-hash order of two `DeclaredFunction`s (`ApiTypeExtractor.scala:116-122`; `DeclaredFunction.java:25`, no `hashCode`). Any run that asks the JVM for identity hashes at other moments before the index is built can flip that order: an audit copy, JFR, another stage's earlier components, a changed memo pattern. Since H the syntax tree no longer moves anything (F-232), so a lone move of `:130` is row 737's and nothing else's. Neither S's memos nor K's fix changed an answer: S's audits found 0 differences, and K's fix computes no hash of a node. Repairing row 737 by matching parameter types takes `:130` out for good. By "Type Inference for Components" `BIG LEXICO(g)` takes `TotalComparison` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:98`), so the count would read 38 and the distance 48.

content.content:
\section{Intersection and Union Types}
\seclabel{internal-types}

For every finite set of types, there is a type denoting a unique
\emph{intersection} of those types.
The intersection of a set of types $S$ is a subtype of every type $T \in S$
and of the intersection of every subset of $S$.
There is also a type denoting a unique \emph{union}
of those types. The union of a set of types $S$ is a supertype of every
type $T \in S$ and of the union of every subset of $S$.
Neither intersection types nor union types are first-class types;
they are used solely for type inference (as described in
  \chapref{type-inference}) and
they cannot be expressed directly in programs.

The intersection of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
any subtype of every type $T \in S$ and of the intersection of every
subset of $S$ is a subtype of $U$.
Similarly, the union of a set of types $S$ is equal to a named type $U$ when
any supertype of every type $T \in S$ and of the union of every
subset of $S$ is a supertype of $U$.

A type $U$ \emph{covers} a type $T$ when every value of $T$ is a value of $U$.
A type covers each of its subtypes, and a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause
is covered by the union of the types listed in the clause
(\secref{trait-decls}).
Covering is a relation between the values of types and not the subtype
relation: a type may cover another type that is not its subtype.
\revision{revival-covering}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not define
covering.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) names covering beside
subtyping and exclusion as a relation between types, and says that an
instantiation of a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is covered by the union of
the listed types.}
For example:
%trait S comprises {U,V} end
%trait T comprises {V,W} end
%trait U extends S excludes W end
%trait V extends {S,T} end
%trait W extends T end
\begin{Fortress}

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations} asks the argument types of the concrete
declarations to cover the argument type of the abstract declaration, where it
asked their union to equal it, and, in its example, for a definition for every
type listed in the \KWD{comprises} clause of \TYP{Molecule} or definitions that
together cover those types, where it asked for one for every immediate subtype.
Each of these four passages has a box.
The draft note says ``all its listed types'' where it said ``all its immediate
subtraits''; a draft note prints only in a draft build, so it has no box.
The effect of \secref{revival-comprises} no longer says that these passages are
not revised.
A correction of 9~October 2026 changes the last sentence of the box after the
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
and \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/comprises-type-level-judgement.md} in the
revival's repository.
The sentence that the correction of 9~October 2026 changes was false when it was
written: since 6~June 2012 the team's compiled type checker, testing whether an
abstract method's parameter type is a subtype of the union of the parameter
types of the concrete methods below it, tests whether the union of the types
that a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause lists is a subtype of that union
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala}
and \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala},
in the revival's repository).
It accepts an object whose methods over the two types that a trait lists cover
an abstract method over that trait, and refuses the same object when the trait
has no \KWD{comprises} clause.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-override/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
The amendment of 14~October 2026 follows the revival's decision of 13~October
2026 that an object defines an inherited abstract method when its definitions
of that name at narrower parameter types together cover the abstract method's
parameter types, \KWD{comprises} clauses read as the compiled type checker
reads them; a definition at the abstract method's own parameter type is the
plain case.
It is the type group's rule of 2012.
The compiled type checker checks, at each object declaration, whether each
inherited abstract method ``is covered by one or more concrete definitions'',
its parameter type a subtype of the union of theirs (Steele, May 2012, in
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/AbstractMethodChecker.scala},
in the revival's repository), and reads \KWD{comprises} clauses to do so since
6~June 2012.
Welterweight Fortress uses the same rules to check methods as functions, the
type of the trait or object within which the method is declared not considered
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Welterweight/static.tick}, lines 27--47).
The sentence of \secref{methods} is older than that reading; the chapter's own
sentence on overloaded functional methods points to
\secref{abstractFunctionDeclarations}, which asks for coverage, as the Meet Rule
429:2. A trait with a comprises clause is considered to have a concrete method declaration with a particular signature even if its declaration is actually abstract provided that all its listed types are considered to have concrete method declaration with that signature.  Thus, such a trait can have a method declaration that is abstract in the component, but not so declared in the API.  (And we might also allow the analogous thing for top-level functions.)

data.summary:
Rung C is approved. The four checker repairs do what the section asks, and the record is true apart from one citation.

- Row 737: ApiTypeExtractor now takes the one api declaration whose parameter types equal the function's. The comparison is ExportChecker.equalTypes, and all three first-pick sites in isExported are repaired.
- Row 738: the message tests traitOrObject.
- Row 739: a component's top-level set now reads abstract functional methods, with an implemented filter found through the declaring traits' ancestors.
- Row 681: isNatTerm now holds any size with no inference variable in it.

The count stage, run again on the base build and the worker's head, took 77 s and 85 s (the worker's were 74 s and 81 s). The tables differ only by #total 39 to 38. The run.txt files differ by :130 alone, and both equal the worker's base and change3 files. The distance files show 49 to 48 with only :130 gone.

The transcript shows the tests failing on the base (14:31:33, before the first edit at 14:35:34) and passing after the last code change (15:07:40, 'OK (16 tests)'). The worker's testQuick on 9697e3838 was 'BUILD SUCCESSFUL'.

I ran 21 programs on old and new code, compiled and under walk. Every change moves toward the specification's answer: a crash becomes PASS, size inference now agrees with walk, and the generic abstract top-level case is refused like its concrete twin. One quiet value is new: a nat inferred as i-1 is -1 at i=0 on the compiled path, where walk refuses it. That is row 675's mechanism, and the written form does the same on the base.

My commits change no code:
- REPORT.md's problem line pointed to batch-16-review.md:21; the quoted sentence is at :25.

- A note for row 675.
